answer.rationale: Rollback is off the table: the 2-hour-old release carries a security patch compliance has ruled non-revertible, so memory_b1's clean rollback precedent is unusable regardless of how well it worked. Capacity work (memory_b3) and read-replica routing (memory_b5) are both mismatched to the signal: the degradation is confined to the primary region and is on the write path, which argues against a global capacity shortfall and against read contention as the driver. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) fail fast, which contains blast radius but sheds exactly the settlement writes we are told not to lose. That leaves regional failover, which matches the one hard localizing fact we have. But memory_b2 is the single memory my choice rests on, and it is the one I know least about in the ways that matter here: the March degradation may have been read-dominated, at low traffic, or with replication lag near zero — none of which describes daily-peak heavy writes. 'Traffic shifted cleanly and error rates recovered' is a latency/error claim, not a durability claim; it says nothing about whether in-flight writes survived. So I want the archived source for memory_b2 specifically to see write mix, replication lag at cutover, and whether any writes were lost or replayed. Downstream risk is real and I am flagging it: failing over a write primary under peak load can drop or duplicate in-flight settlement writes and can move the bottleneck rather than remove it if the cause is a release-induced write-path regression that travels with the build to the secondary region. That last possibility is not ruled out by anything I know — the timing (release 2h ago, climb 90m) is suggestive, and if true, failover buys nothing and costs write integrity. Hence a small guarded test rather than a full cutover: shift a bounded slice of write traffic to the secondary with replication lag gating and a hard abort, and watch whether p99 on the shifted slice tracks target or reproduces the regression. That single probe discriminates between 'regional infrastructure fault' and 'release regression that follows the code,' which is the fork I cannot currently resolve. If verification shows memory_b2's precedent was write-heavy and lossless, I widen within the same window; if it was a read-path event, I hold and treat the release-regression hypothesis as live.
